Medea. Euripides' shocking tragedy of abandonment, revenge, and a woman who commits an act so unspeakable it still shocks audiences twenty-five centuries later.

Medea is a foreign sorceress, a princess from Colchis who sacrificed everything for Jason. She helped him win the Golden Fleece, left her home and family behind, and bore him two sons in Corinth. She gave him everything. And now, seeking political advancement, Jason plans to marry the king's daughter and leave Medea aside.

At first, she contemplates suicide. But suicide would leave Jason victorious, free to marry his new bride and forget her. So she turns to revenge instead—a revenge so complete it will destroy everything he values.

She poisons a wedding gift: a robe and diadem. They kill the young princess and burn down the palace, consuming the king as well. But poison and fire are not enough. The children—Jason's heirs, his legacy, his future—must die too. With a dagger, Medea kills her own sons.

She then escapes in a dragon-drawn chariot, leaving Jason with nothing. No heirs. No legacy. Only the knowledge that his former wife has unmade him completely.

The play is almost unbearable to watch. Yet Euripides forces us to understand Medea even as we recoil from her. She's no simple villain. The nurse and chorus emphasize her isolation as a foreign woman in a Greek city, sympathize with her humiliation, recognize the injustice of Jason's betrayal. She speaks with eloquence and intelligence about her own suffering. She is rational, not mad. She knows exactly what she's doing and why.

The play shattered contemporary norms. A woman is the protagonist. She is neither punished directly nor absolved. She escapes, vindicated in her own mind. Euripides refuses to let his audience look away or condemn too easily. Medea forces us to see how far a justified humiliation can drive a human being, and what monstrosity can wear the mask of reason.
